title: The Half-Blood Prince
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 15 of 40
content:
I returned Snape's old Potions book with three paper markers tucked between the pages.

He removed each one as if they were insects.

“What are these?”

“Questions.”

“I did not invite annotations.”

“They aren't annotations. They're removable.”

“You have introduced foreign material into a thirty-year-old book.”

“They're paper.”

“So are bookworms' preferred meals.”

“Are you comparing my questions to parasites?”

“I am comparing your organizational habits to infestation.”

I sat across from him.

“First marker. Why 'Half-Blood Prince'?”

His expression closed.

I had expected that.

“You may refuse.”

He looked at me sharply.

“Then why ask?”

“Because you may not.”

He leaned back.

The book rested between us.

“Prince was my mother's name.”

“I know that much.”

“Of course you do. Newspapers have excavated my genealogy with all the delicacy of grave robbers.”

“They say your father was a Muggle.”

“He was.”

“And you were proud of your mother's name?”

Snape's fingers touched the cover.

“Pride is a childish word for it.”

“You were a child.”

His gaze lifted.

That stopped him.

“At first,” he said.

I waited.

He looked past me toward the classroom shelves.

“Prince sounded like something chosen instead of inherited. Something that belonged to magic rather than that house.”

Spinner's End.

The narrow bedroom.

The gray street.

“I could be clever there,” he continued. “In the margins. No one knew who had written them. No one cared what I wore, or where I lived, or whose son I was.”

“Only whether the method worked.”

“Yes.”

I understood that more than I wanted to admit.

“So you made yourself a title.”

“A pretentious one.”

“You were a teenager.”

“That is not a defense.”

“It is for pretension.”

His mouth twitched.

“Second marker,” I said.

He sighed with theatrical suffering.

“You corrected a strengthening solution by reducing the powdered griffin claw. Why?”

“Because too much causes brittleness in enchanted tissue.”

“That's not in any reference I own.”

“Then your references are incomplete.”

“How did you discover it?”

“Experiment.”

“At sixteen?”

“Seventeen.”

“Much more sensible.”

His eyebrow rose.

I turned the book toward him.

“You were doing original research before leaving school.”

“I was bored.”

“That is not normal boredom.”

“I have never been accused of normality.”

“True.”

The third marker was the dangerous one.

I hesitated before opening to it.

Sectumsempra.

The word sat in the margin like a scar.

Snape's face hardened.

“You said later,” I reminded him.

“I did.”

“This is later.”

“So it is.”

I did not ask why he invented it first.

I asked, “How old were you?”

“Sixteen.”

My stomach tightened.

“What does it feel like to know something that violent came from you?”

He stared at me.

“That is not the question people ask.”

“What do they ask?”

“Whether I regret it.”

“Do you?”

“Yes.”

No hesitation.

The answer made the next question harder.

“Would you erase it if you could?”

His eyes narrowed.

“No.”

I waited.

“Why?”

“Because erasing the spell from my past would not erase the person who needed to invent it.”

I went still.

Snape's voice was quiet.

“I was angry. Humiliated. Fascinated by Dark magic. Surrounded by people who rewarded cruelty when it was clever enough. And I wanted a weapon that belonged to me.”

“Against the Marauders?”

“Against enemies.”

The old note.

For enemies.

“That included them?”

“Yes.”

“But not only them.”

“No.”

I traced the edge of the page with my gaze.

“Harry used it on Draco.”

Snape's jaw tightened.

“Yes.”

“You saved Draco.”

“Yes.”

“What was that like?”

His eyes flashed.

“Do you collect impossible questions?”

“Professionally.”

He looked at the book.

“To watch a curse I had made cut a boy who had no idea what it was,” he said slowly, “was clarifying.”

“Did you blame Harry?”

“Yes.”

“Did you blame yourself?”

“Yes.”

“Did you tell him what the spell did afterward?”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because I was furious. Because he had stolen from me. Because I was protecting the identity of the Prince. Because I was not, contrary to your developing mythology, always wise.”

“I have no such mythology.”

“You have begun to look at me as though every unpleasant act conceals an admirable motive.”

The accusation stung because it was partly true.

I sat back.

“Thank you.”

His brow furrowed.

“For what?”

“For catching me.”

He looked genuinely confused.

“I don't want to make you easier than you are,” I said. “Not by turning everything into evidence for your guilt, and not by turning everything into evidence for your goodness.”

His gaze sharpened.

“You believe there is a difference.”

“Yes.”

“Between what?”

“Understanding you and excusing you.”

The room went quiet.

Snape's fingers remained on the book.

“Most people prefer one of two stories,” he said at last. “Monster or martyr.”

“Both are lazy.”

“A sentiment you will find unpopular.”

“I have survived worse.”

“So I gather.”

I closed the book.

“Do you still think of yourself as the Half-Blood Prince?”

His expression shifted.

“No.”

“Never?”

“Rarely.”

“What does it mean now?”

He considered.

“A boy who thought invention could make him untouchable.”

“That is sad.”

“It is accurate.”

“Both can be true.”

His eyes met mine.

“Yes.”

That phrase again.

Both can be true.

It had become something between us.

Not forgiveness.

Not absolution.

A refusal to flatten.

Snape slid the book toward himself, then stopped.

“You may keep it another week.”

I blinked.

“You're serious?”

“I am beginning to doubt the wisdom of it.”

“I'll take excellent care of it.”

“You will use no additional markers.”

“I make no promises.”

“Then give it back.”

I pulled it against my chest.

“Too late.”

His eyes narrowed.

I smiled.

For a moment, he looked less like a former spy, former Headmaster, former Death Eater, former boy who had invented a curse for enemies.

He looked like a man watching someone steal his book and deciding, against every instinct, to allow it.

“Insufferable,” he said.

“Pretentious.”

“Thief.”

“Prince.”

That stopped him.

The word hung there, stripped of legend.

Not title.

Not accusation.

Something gentler.

His face changed.

I felt heat rise into mine and looked down too late.

Snape noticed.

Of course he did.

He said nothing.

Later, alone in my room, I opened the book again and studied the handwriting instead of the spells.

Some notes were impatient corrections. Some were elegant improvements. Some were jokes so dry I could hear his adult voice in them. Others made my skin crawl.

That combination mattered.

It would have been easier if brilliance and cruelty occupied separate pages. Easier if there were a chapter where the lonely child ended and the dangerous young man began. The margins refused that comfort.

The next morning I returned the book to him open to a modified potion instruction.

“This one,” I said. “Why twelve clockwise stirs instead of the printed seven?”

His suspicion gave way to interest almost instantly.

“The author assumes a uniform cauldron wall temperature.”

“And yours doesn't?”

“No real cauldron does.”

For ten minutes he forgot to be guarded. He drew a diagram. He explained convection. He became animated enough to steal my quill and correct my notation.

Then he seemed to realize what had happened and stopped.

I looked at the diagram.

“You like this.”

“Competence?”

“Potions.”

His expression closed halfway.

“Yes,” he said.

Not loved. Not once. Just yes.

It was enough to make the room feel brighter.

That silence had a new language too.

prose_fingerprint: emotionally direct without flattening emotion into exposition
ground abstract feelings in concrete physical details, objects, weather, rooms, gestures, and sensory anchors
alternate compact emotional beats with fuller reflective paragraphs
let dialogue carry relationship pressure while narration carries interior consequence
use humor and ordinary practical actions to make vulnerable scenes feel lived-in rather than staged
favor character-specific reactions and small remembered details over generic declarations
allow grief, identity, survival, belonging, home, change, vulnerability, care, and autonomy to recur as thematic pressure
end scenes or chapters on an emotional consequence, changed understanding, concrete image, callback, or forward pull
preserve first-person immediacy and avoid omniscient knowledge outside Jasper's perception
use semicolons selectively for linked thoughts rather than mechanically
dialogue_fingerprint: continuous dialogue should sound conversational rather than like alternating speeches
interrupt dialogue with gestures, environment, hesitation, humor, and internal reaction
let characters dodge, misunderstand, tease, repair, and return to earlier wording
do not make every character equally eloquent, equally dominant, or equally emotionally transparent
relationship_fingerprint: slow burn must accumulate evidence: remembered preferences, repaired conflict, shared routines, private jokes, and practical care
attraction should not erase plot, outside obligations, individual goals, or conflict
vulnerability is strongest when it changes later behavior
after an intense/private interlude, resume with reconnection, humor, care, consequences, memory updates, and the next plot beat rather than treating intimacy as a reset
